claims.claim: Good people who never heard of Christ can still be saved.

stances.summary: Christ is the Word, and every race of people has a share in Him. So those who lived by that Word before He came, like Socrates and Heraclitus, were Christians, even if people called them atheists.
stances.quote: We have been taught that Christ is the first-born of God, and we have declared above that He is the Word of whom every race of men were partakers; and those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists; as, among the Greeks, Socrates and Heraclitus, and men like them
stances.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written about 155 to the emperor Antoninus Pius. Justin is answering an objection: if salvation comes through a Christ born only 150 years earlier, was everyone born before Him "irresponsible"? His whole case is about people who lived BEFORE Christ. He says nothing here about people living after Christ who never hear of Him. The "reason" he means is the Logos, the Word, which is Christ; to live "reasonably" is to live by the Word. The Second Apology says the same: Christ "was partially known even by Socrates (for He was and is the Word who is in every man" (chapter 10), and "Whatever things were rightly said among all men, are the property of us Christians" (chapter 13). But the philosophers had only a "seed" of the Word, not the whole. In the Dialogue with Trypho 45 he says those who did "that which is universally, naturally, and eternally good" before and under the law "shall be saved through this Christ in the resurrection". So for Justin such people are saved through Christ, not apart from Him. Orthodox; martyred in Rome about 165.

stances.summary: God condemns no one unheard. The good who died before Christ, Greeks who lived by philosophy and Jews who lived by the law, heard the gospel after death, when the Lord and then the apostles preached in Hades. All who believed there were saved.
stances.quote: For it is not right that these should be condemned without trial, and that those alone who lived after the advent should have the advantage of the divine righteousness.
stances.context: Written about 200 in Alexandria. "These" are the souls who died before Christ came, "not having the Gospel preached to them". Clement reads 1 Peter 3:19-20 to mean the gospel was preached in Hades, "so that even there, all the souls, on hearing the proclamation, might either exhibit repentance, or confess that their punishment was just". So in his view no one is saved without ever hearing; the hearing comes after death. He adds that God and the Lord "save with a righteousness and equality which extend to all that turn to Him, whether here or elsewhere", and that God's punishments "are saving and disciplinary". He offers the apostles' preaching in Hades as his own opinion ("as I think", "in my opinion"). In Stromata 1.5 he says: "before the advent of the Lord, philosophy was necessary to the Greeks for righteousness", a schoolmaster to bring them to Christ. Chrysostom later rejects the idea of salvation after death (see his entry). Clement speaks only of those who died before Christ.

stances.summary: Christ did not come only for the people of His own time. He came for everyone from the beginning who feared and loved God, treated others justly, and longed to see Him. He will raise them and give them a place in His kingdom.
stances.quote: for all men altogether, who from the beginning, according to their capacity, in their generation have both feared and loved God, and practised justice and piety towards their neighbours, and have earnestly desired to see Christ, and to hear His voice.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885
stances.context: Written about 180. The sentence begins: "For it was not merely for those who believed on Him in the time of Tiberius Cæsar that Christ came, nor did the Father exercise His providence for the men only who are now alive, but". The people in view are the righteous before Christ, chiefly patriarchs and prophets who "earnestly desired to see Christ". Book 4, chapter 27, section 2 says Christ went down to preach to those who "had hope towards Him", namely "the righteous men, the prophets, and the patriarchs". So they were not people who knew nothing of Him; they looked forward to Him. He also holds that the Word always revealed God: "For the Son, being present with His own handiwork from the beginning, reveals the Father to all; to whom He wills, and when He wills, and as the Father wills" (4.6.7). Nothing here on people after Christ who never hear. Orthodox; bishop of Lyons.

stances.original: iste licet alienus a vita videatur aeterna, quia non credit Christo, et intrare non possit in regnum coelorum, quia renatus non est ex aqua et Spiritu, videtur tamen quod per haec quae dicuntur ab Apostolo, bonorum operum gloriam, et honorem, et pacem perdere penitus non possit.
stances.summary: A pagan who does good by nature, keeping justice, chastity and self-control, cannot enter the kingdom without faith in Christ and new birth. But he will not lose the reward of his good works. And outside the Church no one is saved.
stances.quote: Though he seems a stranger to eternal life, because he does not believe in Christ, and cannot enter the kingdom of heaven, because he has not been born again of water and the Spirit, yet it seems from what the Apostle says that he cannot wholly lose the glory, honour and peace of his good works.
stances.translation: Own rendering from Rufinus's Latin (Migne, Patrologia Graeca 14, 1857)
stances.work: Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans (Latin version by Rufinus)
stances.location: Book 2, section 7, on Romans 2:10 (Migne, Patrologia Graeca 14, column 888)
stances.context: Commentary written about 246. The Greek is lost here; the text survives in Rufinus's shortened Latin of about 406, so some wording may be his. The subject (own renderings in this paragraph) is "the Greek, that is, the Gentile" who without the law, "as we see some among the Gentiles", keeps justice, chastity, prudence, temperance and modesty. The only English is modern and copyrighted (Scheck, 2001), hence the own rendering; the Latin was read in the archive.org scan of Migne. Origen holds two things at once: no eternal life or kingdom for such a pagan, yet his good works keep their "glory, honour and peace" (Romans 2:10). Elsewhere he is blunt: "Let no one persuade himself, let no one deceive himself: outside this house, that is, outside the Church, no one is saved" (Homilies on Joshua 3.5, about 249; own rendering of Rufinus's Latin "Nemo ergo sibi persuadeat, nemo semeipsum decipiat: extra hanc domum, id est extra Ecclesiam nemo salvatur", read in Migne, Patrologia Graeca 12). With Cyprian's, this is one of the two earliest forms of the "outside the Church" formula; it uses Rahab's house and is aimed at those who leave the Church and at Jews who reject Christ. Against Celsus 4.7 (ANF vol. 4, Frederick Crombie) adds that God never stopped working for goodness: "in every generation the wisdom of God, passing into those souls which it ascertains to be holy, converts them into friends and prophets of God." Origen also hoped that all might finally be restored to God. HETERODOX: teachings linked to his name were condemned in the sixth century.

stances.summary: Before Christ came, people were saved if they worshipped the one true God, lived well and kept away from idols. Now that He has come, knowing Christ is needed too. But God never overlooks someone who truly seeks Him.
stances.quote: For then it was sufficient for salvation, as I have said already, to know God only; but now it is so no more, but there is need also of the knowledge of Christ.
stances.translation: George Prevost, revised by M. B. Riddle, NPNF 1st series vol. 10, 1888
stances.context: Preached in Antioch about 390. Just before this he says: "By no means, for men might then be saved, even though they had not confessed Christ. For this was not required of them, but not to worship idols, and to know the true God." In the same section he rejects salvation after death (Clement's view): "if unbelievers are after death to be saved on their believing, no man shall ever perish." Homily 5 on Romans (on Romans 2:10) names such God-fearing Gentiles before Christ: "such as were Melchizedek and his (οἱ περὶ), such as was Job, such as were the Ninevites, such as was Cornelius." For people after Christ, Homily 26 on Romans (on Romans 14:23, NPNF 1st series vol. 11) takes up the question: "Say not then, how came God to neglect such and such a one who was no formalist (ἄ πλαστος) and a good man, though a Gentile?" Only God knows who is truly sincere, he replies, and Cornelius and Abraham show that God brings the truth to the earnest: "For it is impossible in the extreme, that the sober-minded (νήφοντα) should ever be overlooked." So in his view a truly good person will not be left unreached. Orthodox; archbishop of Constantinople.

stances.summary: Some outsiders already live the Christian life and lack only the name. His own father was one of them, and his good life was rewarded by coming to faith.
stances.quote: Even before he was of our fold, he was ours. His character made him one of us. For, as many of our own are not with us, whose life alienates them from the common body, so, many of those without are on our side, whose character anticipates their faith, and need only the name of that which indeed they possess.
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894
stances.work: Oration 18, Funeral Oration on his Father
stances.context: Preached in 374 at his father's funeral. His father had belonged to the Hypsistarians, a sect that mixed Jewish and Greek practice and, Gregory says, worshipped only "the Almighty" (section 5); he was baptized about 325. So the man praised was not someone who never heard; he was an outsider who later believed. Gregory goes on: "It was as a reward for such conduct, I think, that he attained to the faith." This is praise in a eulogy, not a doctrine of salvation. On people who die unbaptized through no fault of their own he gives a middle answer in Oration 40.23 (381): "the third will be neither glorified nor punished by the righteous Judge, as unsealed and yet not wicked, but persons who have suffered rather than done wrong." There he means infants and people prevented by circumstance, not pagans. Orthodox; one of the Cappadocian Fathers.

stances.summary: The souls who lived before Christ were not abandoned. God's kindness reached them too, and they were delivered. But no one now reaches eternal life except by Christ's gift.
stances.quote: The Lord's compassion has been shown to them, too, and the divine kindness has been extended to all alike; they have been preserved, have been delivered
stances.translation: Hamilton Bryce and Hugh Campbell, ANF vol. 6, 1886
stances.context: Written about 300 by a North African teacher of rhetoric soon after his conversion; his theology is idiosyncratic. He answers the pagan question "of what crime were former ages guilty which were cut off in their mortal state before He came?" He first says we cannot know, then says the ancients were preserved and delivered. (The sentence ends "the lot and. condition of mortality", a typo on the page.) For his own hearers he is strict: "by no efforts will you be able to reach the prize of immortality, unless by Christ's gift you have perceived what constitutes this very immortality" (2.66). Not in the candidate pool. Lactantius was his pupil.

stances.summary: The righteous from the first man to Abraham were Christians in everything but the name. They lived the same life and knew the same Christ, who appeared to them.
stances.quote: If any one should assert that all those who have enjoyed the testimony of righteousness, from Abraham himself back to the first man, were Christians in fact if not in name, he would not go beyond the truth.
stances.translation: Arthur Cushman McGiffert, NPNF 2nd series vol. 1, 1890
stances.context: Written about 312-325. His point is that Christianity is the oldest religion, not a new one. He adds that these men "also clearly knew the very Christ of God; for it has already been shown that he appeared unto Abraham" (1.4.8). So they are not people who never heard of Christ; they knew Him before His birth. He speaks only of the biblical patriarchs. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.summary: There is no salvation outside the Church. Not even dying as a martyr saves someone who is outside it.
stances.quote: But if not even the baptism of a public confession and blood can profit a heretic to salvation, because there is no salvation out of the Church
stances.work: Letter 72, to Jubaianus (Letter 73 in modern numbering)
stances.context: Written in 256, in the dispute over rebaptizing converts from heretical groups. His targets are heretics and schismatics who knew Christ but stood outside the Catholic Church, not pagans who never heard. The Latin is usually given as "salus extra ecclesiam non est" (not checked here). The same view in On the Unity of the Church 6 (251): "He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his mother. If any one could escape who was outside the Ark of Noah, then he also may escape who shall be outside of the Church." On pagan virtue he is dismissive: "Philosophers also profess that they pursue this virtue; but in their case the patience is as false as their wisdom also is" (On the Advantage of Patience 2). He never discusses people who had no chance to hear. Orthodox; bishop of Carthage; martyred 258.

stances.summary: Even a naturally kind and generous person gains nothing without knowing God. Knowing God is the head; virtues without it are a body without a head, with no life in it.
stances.quote: such a man as we have heard that Cimon was at Athens, who both gave alms to the needy, and entertained the poor, and clothed the naked; yet, when that one thing which is of the greatest importance is wanting — the acknowledgment of God — then all those good things are superfluous and empty, so that in pursuing them he has laboured in vain.
stances.context: Written about 303-311. The sentence opens: "But let us suppose it possible that any one, by natural and innate goodness, should gain true virtues". Cimon was an Athenian general of the fifth century BC, famous for his generosity. Lactantius goes on: "This is the reason why the philosophers, though they may be naturally good, yet have no knowledge and no intelligence. All their learning and virtue is without a head, because they are ignorant of God". What he requires is "the acknowledgment of God", the one true God, and he ties the hope of immortality to those "who continue in His religion". He does not discuss people who never had the chance to hear. Pupil of Arnobius; tutor to Constantine's son.

stances.original: fuerit salus retro per fidem nudam ante domini passionem et resurrectionem: at ubi fides aucta est, credentibus in nativitatem passionem resurrectionemque eius addita est ampliato sacramento obsignatio baptismi
stances.summary: Before Christ's passion, bare faith could save, as it did Abraham. Now Christ has commanded baptism, and the rule is that no one is saved without it.
stances.quote: Grant that, in days gone by, there was salvation by means of bare faith, before the passion and resurrection of the Lord. But now that faith has been enlarged, and has become a faith which believes in His nativity, passion, and resurrection, there has been an amplification added to the sacrament, viz., the sealing act of baptism
stances.context: Written about 200-206, before his Montanist years. The Latin is from thelatinlibrary.com. Chapter 12 opens: "When, however, the prescript is laid down that without baptism, salvation is attainable by none". He is answering Christians who said faith alone was enough; pagans who never heard are not his subject, so applying this to them is an inference from his rule. His scorn for pagan wisdom shows in On the Shows 30, where at the Judgment he pictures "the very philosophers, in fact, who taught their followers that God had no concern in ought that is sublunary" burning with their followers. His phrase about "the soul by nature Christian" (Apology 17) is about the soul's instinctive witness to one God, not about salvation. LATER HETERODOX: a Montanist from about 207.

stances.summary: If a good life by nature could save, then Christ died for nothing. Even in a far-off nation the gospel has not reached, no one is rescued from God's just judgment except by faith in Christ and His sacrament.
stances.quote: If, however, Christ did not die in vain, then human nature cannot by any means be justified and redeemed from God's most righteous wrath— in a word, from punishment — except by faith and the sacrament of the blood of Christ.
stances.translation: Peter Holmes and Robert Ernest Wallis, revised by Benjamin B. Warfield, NPNF 1st series vol. 5, 1887
stances.context: Written in 415 against Pelagius's book On Nature. In this chapter Augustine raises the case himself: "there are some remote nations still (although it is said they are very few) to whom the preached gospel has not found its way". In chapter 10 he takes "the instance of a young man, or an old man, who has died in a region where he could not hear of the name of Christ", and says that calling such a man righteous by nature makes the cross of no effect. Earlier, in Letter 102 (about 409, NPNF 1st series vol. 1), he is more open about the past: "why may we not believe that in other nations also, here and there, some more were found, although we do not read their names in these authoritative records?" But even there they are saved by believing in Christ, and he adds: "those to whom it has not been preached at all are those who were foreknown as persons who would not believe" (102.15). City of God 18.47 (420s) uses Job, who was not an Israelite, to show "that among other nations also there might be men pertaining to the spiritual Jerusalem who have lived according to God and have pleased Him", but only if "the one Mediator between God and men, the Man Christ Jesus" was revealed to them. Letter 164.4 (414) shows the pull he felt toward admired pagans: "we would desire those in whom they exist, either by special preference or along with the others, to be freed from the pains of hell, were not the verdict of human feeling different from that of the justice of the Creator." City of God 19.25: virtues with no reference to God "are rather vices than virtues". No real change of mind: from 409 on the rule is the same, pressed harder against the Pelagians. Orthodox; bishop of Hippo.

stances.summary: The whole Church teaches that God is truly worshipped only within her, and that no one outside her will be saved.
stances.quote: Now the holy Church universal proclaims that God cannot be truly worshipped saving within herself, asserting that all they that are without her shall never be saved.
stances.translation: Library of the Fathers, Oxford: John Henry Parker, vol. 2 of 3, 1844-1850 (translator not named on the title page)
stances.work: Morals on the Book of Job (Moralia in Job)
stances.context: Written about 579-595. His target is heretics, who reply "is it so, that whosoever is out of thee cannot be saved?" He does not discuss pagans who never heard. Yet he honours Job as a righteous Gentile, "who without the Law lived as by law" (Preface), and also treats Job as a prophet of the Redeemer, so Job is not a man ignorant of Christ. The story that his prayers freed the pagan emperor Trajan from hell is a later legend (see misattributions). The Latin is usually given as "omnes qui extra ipsam sunt, minime salvabuntur" (not checked here). The page breaks lines inside this sentence; compare after collapsing whitespace. Orthodox; pope 590-604.

stances.original: Firmissime tene, et nullatenus dubites, non solum omnes paganos, sed etiam omnes Judaeos, et omnes haereticos atque schismaticos, qui extra Ecclesiam catholicam praesentem finiunt vitam, in ignem aeternum ituros, qui paratus est diabolo et angelis ejus
stances.summary: Hold it as certain: pagans, Jews, heretics and schismatics who die outside the Catholic Church will go into eternal fire.
stances.quote: Hold most firmly and never doubt that not only all pagans, but also all Jews and all heretics and schismatics who end this present life outside the Catholic Church, will go into the eternal fire which was prepared for the devil and his angels.
stances.translation: Own rendering from the Latin (Migne, Patrologia Latina 65)
stances.work: On the Faith, to Peter (De fide ad Petrum)
stances.context: Written about 523 by a North African bishop who followed Augustine; in the Middle Ages the work often went under Augustine's name. It is a rule of faith in short articles that each begin "Firmissime tene" ("hold most firmly"). The next article (80) says a heretic or schismatic cannot be saved outside the Church even if he has shed his blood for the name of Christ ("etsi pro Christi nomine etiam sanguinem fuderit", read in the same scan). The Council of Florence (1442, Cantate Domino) closely follows this wording. The PDF at the url is a scanned image with no text layer; the Latin was read from the page image. It speaks of all pagans without distinction; it does not single out those who never heard. Not in the candidate pool.

stances.original: Eos autem merito torqueri, qui deum nesciunt, ut impios, ut iniustos, nisi profanus nemo deliberat, cum parentem omnium et omnium dominum non minoris sceleris sit ignorare quam laedere.
stances.summary: Those who do not know God are rightly punished as ungodly. Not knowing the Father and Lord of all is as wicked as offending Him.
stances.quote: But that they who know not God are deservedly tormented as impious, as unrighteous persons, no one except a profane man hesitates to believe, since it is not less wicked to be ignorant of, than to offend the Parent of all, and the Lord of all.
stances.context: A Latin dialogue of about 200-240; the Christian speaker, Octavius, voices the author's view. The Latin is from thelatinlibrary.com. The same speaker is generous to the philosophers' ideas: "any one might think either that Christians are now philosophers, or that philosophers were then already Christians" (chapter 20), but that concerns their belief in one God, not their salvation. He continues here: "although ignorance of God is sufficient for punishment, even as knowledge of Him is of avail for pardon". Not in the candidate pool.

splits_fathers: Real voices on both sides, but they mostly answer different questions. The hopeful voices (Justin, Clement, Irenaeus, Arnobius, Eusebius, and Chrysostom about the past) speak of good people who lived BEFORE Christ. They say such people were saved through Christ the Word: He was somehow known to them, or preached to them after death (Clement). For people living AFTER Christ who never hear, almost no early voice says "yes, saved as they are". Origen comes closest: their good works keep a reward, but not eternal life or the kingdom. Chrysostom and Gregory of Nazianzus answer instead that God brings the truly good to faith, so the case should not arise. The strict answer is the majority and hardens with time: Minucius Felix and Lactantius on ignorance of God, Cyprian and Origen's "outside the Church no one is saved", Augustine against the Pelagians, then Fulgentius and Gregory the Great. So: about people before Christ, a real split (Justin and Clement against Minucius Felix and Lactantius). About people after Christ, a near-consensus "no", softened by the conviction that God reaches the sincere.
splits_people_today: Ordinary people today lean strongly to "agree"; most non-Christians find the opposite unfair. Among Christians it is a live split by tradition. Catholic teaching since Vatican II (Lumen Gentium 16, quoted in the Catechism, paragraph 847) says those who through no fault of their own do not know the gospel, but seek God sincerely and try to do His will, may be saved. Many mainline Protestants hold similar or wider hopes, and many Orthodox say they know where the Church is but not where it is not. Many evangelicals and confessional Protestants disagree: the Southern Baptist Baptist Faith and Message (2000) says there is no salvation apart from personal faith in Jesus Christ. US surveys (Pew, 2008) found most American Christians saying some non-Christians can reach eternal life, with evangelicals more divided (from memory; check figures before citing). A weak discriminator for the general public, a strong one among committed Christians.

misattributions.line: Extra ecclesiam nulla salus (Outside the Church there is no salvation)
misattributions.truth: The idea is Cyprian's but not this exact slogan. His words are usually given as "salus extra ecclesiam non est" (Letter 73.21 in modern numbering; ANF Letter 72.21 renders "there is no salvation out of the Church"). Origen, in Rufinus's Latin, has "extra Ecclesiam nemo salvatur" (Homilies on Joshua 3.5). In Migne's edition of Fulgentius, "Extra Ecclesiam salus nulla" is only an editor's chapter heading (chapter 37), not Fulgentius's text. The compact slogan is a later standard form.

The term is Karl Rahner's (20th century). Justin wrote that "those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists" (First Apology 46), meaning those who lived by the Word before Christ, not people today who never hear.

misattributions.line: The virtues of the pagans are but "splendid vices"
misattributions.truth: The phrase is not in Augustine. It is a later summary of City of God 19.25, where virtues with no reference to God "are rather vices than virtues".

misattributions.line: Gregory the Great's tears and prayers freed the pagan emperor Trajan from hell
misattributions.truth: A legend first told in the anonymous Whitby Life of Gregory (early eighth century) and retold by John the Deacon (ninth century), not anything Gregory wrote. His own Moralia 14.5 says all outside the Church "shall never be saved".

misattributions.line: The soul is by nature Christian (so good pagans are already Christians)
misattributions.truth: The words are real (Apology 17: the testimony of the soul "by nature Christian"), but they describe the soul's instinctive witness to one God. Tertullian draws no conclusion about salvation from it, and elsewhere insists no one is saved without baptism (On Baptism 12-13).

misattributions.line: We know where the Church is; we do not know where it is not
misattributions.attributed_to: often presented as an ancient Orthodox or patristic saying
misattributions.truth: No patristic source is known for it; it is a modern Orthodox saying, popularised by Kallistos Ware's The Orthodox Church (1963).

notes:
1. The key distinction is BEFORE Christ versus AFTER Christ. Almost every "agree" voice is about people who died before Christ came (Socrates, Heraclitus, Job, the patriarchs). If the quiz statement is read as "people today who never hear", the early Church is nearly unanimous for "disagree", with Origen, Chrysostom and Gregory of Nazianzus giving softer middle answers. Worth deciding which reading the item intends; a statement about "people who lived before Jesus" would split the Fathers far better.
2. "Good" is contested in itself. Lactantius (virtue without God is a body without a head), Cyprian (the philosophers' patience "is as false as their wisdom") and Augustine (City of God 19.25) deny that pagan virtue is true virtue at all; Chrysostom says only God knows who is truly sincere.
3. No stance for Pelagius. His Letter to Demetrias 3 (Latin read in the archive.org scan of Migne, Patrologia Latina 30, where it sits among works once credited to Jerome) praises chaste, patient, generous philosophers as proof of nature's goodness: "Unde, quaeso, hominibus alienis a Deo placent? Unde autem illis bona nisi de naturae bono?" ("Where, I ask, does it come from that men who are strangers to God please us? Where do their good things come from, if not from the goodness of nature?", own rendering). He does not say there that they are saved. Augustine argues that Pelagius's view implies it (On Nature and Grace 2 and 10), but that is Augustine's reading, not Pelagius's words.
4. Leads NOT verified, do not use without checking: Augustine, Against Julian 4.3.25-26 (421), is widely cited as saying the virtuous Roman Fabricius will be punished less than Catiline, not because he was good but because Catiline was worse; the Latin site augustinus.it refused automated access. Augustine, Retractations 1.13.3, on "the Christian religion" existing among the ancients before Christ. Ambrose, On the Death of Valentinian 51-53 (392), hopes an emperor who died unbaptized was saved by his desire for baptism; that is about a catechumen, not someone who never heard. Prosper of Aquitaine, The Call of All Nations, on a general grace given to all peoples. Gregory of Nyssa, Macrina (On the Soul and the Resurrection) and Isaac the Syrian hoped for the final restoration of all, which makes the question moot, but no text found addresses the never-heard as such.
5. No position found (not an exhaustive search) for Ignatius, Perpetua, Hippolytus, Novatian, Antony, Athanasius, Ephrem, Hilary, Basil, Gregory of Nyssa, Macrina, Syncletica, Moses the Black, Arsenius, Poemen, Evagrius, Ambrose, Jerome, Cassian, Martin, Paulinus, Benedict, Boethius, Climacus or Isaac.
6. Checking: all English quotations were copied from the raw newadvent.org and lectionarycentral.com pages and matched by script after collapsing whitespace. The Greek words inside the Chrysostom context may be encoded differently on the page. The two own renderings (Origen, Fulgentius) point to scans: Origen's to the archive.org OCR text of Migne; Fulgentius's to a PDF with no text layer. WebSearch was unavailable during this research (session budget spent), so sources were reached by known URLs and the archive.org catalogue.
